Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 1:

﴿Ṣād﴾ We have discussed the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijā’, the letters that open some surahs) in al-Baqarah. This surah has a distinctive feature: it is said of it that the meaning is "Ṣadaqa Muḥammad" (Muhammad has spoken the truth). It is also said that it is a letter from the Name of Allah, al-Ṣamad, or from ṣādiq al-wa‘d (the One who is true to His promise), or from ṣāni‘ al-maṣnū‘āt (the Maker of created things). ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾. This is an oath whose response is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Indeed the Qur'an is from Allah, and indeed Muhammad is truthful," and what is similar to that. It is also said that its response is in His saying ﴿Ṣād﴾, since it has the meaning "Ṣadaqa Muḥammad." It is also said that its response is [the one that follows]: ﴿Each one of them did not do other than deny the messengers﴾ [Ṣ: 14], but this is far-fetched. It is also said that its response is ﴿Indeed that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Ṣ: 64], and this is even more far-fetched. The meaning of "dhī al-dhikr" (full of reminder) is honour (al-sharaf), and dhikr here means admonition (al-mawi‘ah), or the remembrance of Allah and what is needed of the sacred law (al-sharī‘ah).

Translation:

﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition.﴾ "Those who disbelieve" means the Quraysh. "Bal" (rather, nay) is used to turn away from a omitted statement, which is the response to the oath; that is: their disbelief is not based on proof, but rather it is due to arrogance (ʿizzah) and opposition (shiqaq). ʿIzzah means haughtiness, and shiqaq means enmity and the intention of contradicting. Their being indefinite (nakirah) indicates the intensity of both, and the magnification of the disbelievers in them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 3:

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them!﴾ An informative statement that contains a threat to Quraysh. ﴿Then they cried out, but it was no time for escape.﴾ The meaning is that the generations who were destroyed called out and sought help when that did not benefit them. "Lāta" (لات) means "laysa" (ليس, "it is not"), and it is "lā" (لا, the negative particle) to which the feminine marker has been added, just as it was added in "rubbat" (ربت) and "thamma" (ثمة). Lāta only enters upon a time expression, and its subject is an implied pronoun, and "ḥīna manāṣ" (حين مناص) is its predicate. The implied sense is: "The time in which they called out was not a time of escape." And "al-manāṣ" (المناص) means the flight and deliverance, from your saying: "nāṣa yanūṣu" (ناص ينوص), meaning he fled.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verses 4–5:

﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Quraysh, and the warner is our master Muhammad (ﷺ). That is, they found it improbable that God would send a messenger from among them. It may also mean from their own tribe, or it may mean from among mankind, being like them. ﴿And the disbelievers say﴾ The original form would have been "and they said," but the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun deliberately, to describe them as disbelievers. ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ This is their denial of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness).

The occasion of revelation of these verses was that the Quraysh gathered and said to Abu Talib: "Restrain your nephew from us, for he finds fault with our religion, disparages our gods, and makes foolish our minds." So Abu Talib spoke to him about this, and he (ﷺ) said: "I only want from them one word, by which they would rule the non-Arabs, and by which the Arabs would submit to them." They said: "Yes, and ten words along with it." He said: "Say, there is no god but God." So they stood up, denied that, and said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

And the eminent among them went forth, saying, "Walk on and be steadfast in your gods; indeed, this is a thing that is intended." (﴿وَٱنطَلَقَ ٱلْمَلأُ مِنْهُمْ أَنِ ٱمْشُواْ وَاْصْبِرُواْ﴾ ﴿إِنَّ هَـٰذَا لَشَيْءٌ يُرَادُ﴾)

The "going forth" of the eminent (al-mala') is an expression for their leaving Abu Talib. It was also said: it is an expression for their scattering through the streets of Makkah and spreading disbelief. As for "walk on" (an-imshu): its meaning is that some of them said to others, "Walk on and be steadfast in the worship of your gods, and do not obey Muhammad in what he calls you to, namely the worship of God alone." ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended.﴾ This too is among the words of the Quraysh that Allah related, and it has two possible meanings. The first: the reference is to Islam and tawhid, i.e. this monotheism is a thing that is desired of us to submit to. The second: the reference is to polytheism and steadfastness toward their gods, i.e. this thing ought to be desired and held fast to; or that this is a thing which Allah wills of us, since He has decreed it upon us. The first is more preferable, because the reference that follows is to it, so the speech stays in one consistent line.

"We have not heard of this in the latter religion" (ما سمعنا بهذا في الملة الآخرة). This too is part of what God relates of their speech: that is, "We have not heard of monotheism (tawhid) in the latter religion." By "the latter religion" (al-milla al-akhira) some mean the religion of the Christians, since it comes after that of Moses and others, and they affirm the Trinity, not monotheism. It was also said that it means the religion of Quraysh: that is, "We have not heard of this in the religion upon which we found our fathers." And it was said that it means the awaited religion, since they used to hear from the rabbis and soothsayers that a messenger would be sent who would be the last of the prophets.

﴿Ina hadha illa ikhtilaq﴾ ("This is nothing but a fabrication"). This too is part of what is related of their speech, and the reference is to monotheism and Islam. The meaning of ikhtilaq (fabrication) is lying.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 8:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us?﴾ The hamza here is for denial (al-inkar), and the meaning is that they denied that God would single out Muhammad ﷺ for the revelation of the Qur'an over them. ﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder.﴾ This is a rebuttal of them: the meaning is that they have no proof (hujjah) and no evidence (burhan), but rather they are in doubt about the knowledge of God and His oneness, and that is why they disbelieved. It is also possible that by "the Reminder" he means the Qur'an. ﴿Nay, but they have not yet tasted My punishment.﴾ This is a warning (wa'id) and a threat to them. The meaning is that what led them to disbelief is that they have not yet tasted the punishment; when they taste it, their doubt will be removed and they will submit to the truth.

Verse 9: ﴿Or do they possess the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾

This is a rebuttal of their denial of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) being singled out for prophethood. The meaning is that they do not possess the treasuries of Allah's mercy, so that they could give prophethood to whomever they wish and withhold it from whomever they wish. Rather, Allah gives it to whomever He wills. Then He described Himself as the Almighty (al-'Aziz), who does what He wills, and the Bestower (al-Wahhab), who grants to whomever He wills. Therefore they have no proof for what they denied.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 10:

﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them?﴾ This is also a refutation of them. The meaning: Do they have dominion so that they may dispose of it as they wish? Rather, the Owner of the dominion does in His dominion what He wills. The first "am" (أم) is disjunctive, meaning "rather," together with the interrogative hamza of denial. As for the second "am" (أم), it may be the same, or it may be a conjunctive "am" (عاطفة معادلة) corresponding to what precedes it.

﴿Then let them climb up by the ropes.﴾ This is a challenge to them and a mockery of them. "Yartaqu" (يرتقوا) means "let them ascend." "Al-asbab" (الأسباب) here means ladders and paths, and what is similar to them, that by which one reaches a height. It was also said: they are the gates of heaven. The meaning: if they have dominion over the heavens and the earth, then let them ascend to the Throne and manage the kingdom.

This is a warning of their defeat in battle; they were defeated at Badr and elsewhere. "Ma hunalika" is a descriptive clause (sifah) qualifying "jund" (troops), and it carries the sense of belittling them. The reference of "hunalika" (there) is to the state in which they described themselves, namely disbelief and mockery. It was also said that the reference is to the ascent through the means (al-irtiqa' fi al-asbab), but this is far-fetched (ba'id). And it was said that the reference is to the site of Badr. "Min al-ahzab" means: from among the parties (al-ahzab) who were fanatically attached to falsehood and so perished.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 15:

﴿And these do not await but a single blast﴾. Here "yanzur" means "yantazir" (to await). "These" refers to the Quraysh. The "single blast" is the blast in the Trumpet, the blast of swooning (nafkhat al-sa'q). It was also said: the blast refers to what befell them of killing or hardship. The first is more apparent, and it has been related that its interpretation was thus from the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿Without any delay (fawaq)﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions. The first: "mali-ha ruju'" (it has no return), meaning they will not return to the world after it; on this view the word is derived from "ifaqah" (recovering consciousness). The second: "ma la-ha min tarddud" (it has no repetition), meaning it is a single blast with no second. The third: "ma la-ha min ta'khir wa la tawaqquf miqdar fawaq naqah," meaning there is no delay or pause of the length of a she-camel's fawaq, which is the interval between the two milkings. This third opinion applies only to the reading "fuwaq" with a dammah, because the fawaq of the she-camel is with a dammah. The first two opinions apply to both the fathah and the dammah readings.

﴿And they said, "Our Lord, hasten for us our *qiṭṭ*"﴾. The word القط (*al-qiṭṭ*), linguistically, has two meanings. One is: the book (record). The other is: a portion, share. Its meaning here has three opinions:

First: our portion of good, meaning they asked that God hasten it for them in this world.

Second: our portion of punishment. This is like their saying: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the heaven﴾ [al-Anfal: 32].

Third: the pages of our deeds.

﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud (David), the possessor of strength; indeed he was ever turning back (to Allah).﴾ *Al-ayd* means strength. Dawud combined physical strength, strength of religion, sovereignty, and armies. *Al-awwab* means one who returns repeatedly to Allah.

If it is asked: what is the connection between Allah's command to our master Muhammad (ﷺ) to be patient over the words of the disbelievers, and His command to him to mention Dawud? My answer is that the mention of Dawud and of the prophets after him in this surah contains consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), a promise to him of victory and the relief of distress, and help for him in the patience he was commanded to observe. Allah mentioned the blessings He bestowed upon Dawud: the subjugation of birds and mountains, the strength of his kingdom, his being given wisdom and decisive speech, and then his final destiny in the Hereafter, which is nearness (to Allah) and a good return. It is as if He says: "O Muhammad, just as We bestowed these blessings upon Dawud, so We bestow them upon you. So be patient and do not grieve over what they say." Then He mentioned what He gave Sulayman (Solomon) of great sovereignty, the subjugation of the wind and the jinn, and his final destiny of nearness and a good return, and then mentioned those prophets mentioned after that. The purpose is to mention the blessings bestowed upon them in order to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ). Also, Dawud, Sulayman, and Ayyub (Job) were afflicted with hardships, then Allah relieved them and followed these with great good. So He commanded our master Muhammad (ﷺ) to mention them, to teach him that He will relieve him of what he suffers from the harm of his people, and will follow that with victory and dominance over them. Thus the connection in this is clear.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning is: "Remember Dawud, the possessor of strength in religion, so take him as an example and strengthen yourself as he was strengthened."

Al-Zamakhshari answered the question, saying: "It is as if Allah said to His Prophet (ﷺ): 'Be patient over what they say,' and magnify the matter of disobedience in the eyes of the disbelievers by mentioning the story of Dawud. He was a noble prophet with Allah, then he slipped into a slip, for which Allah rebuked him, so he sought forgiveness and turned back. So what do you think of yourselves with your disbelief and your disobedience?" This answer does not conceal the bad manners it contains toward Dawud, peace be upon him, in making him an example through which Allah threatens the disbelievers, and in stating explicitly that he slipped and that Allah rebuked him for his slip. We seek refuge in Allah from mentioning the prophets in such a manner.

﴿And the ishraq﴾: meaning the time of ishraq, which is when the sun rises, that is, when it shines and its rays become yellowish, and this is the time of forenoon (*duha*). As for *shuruq* (its rising), it is its ascent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 20:

﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾. It is said: this means prophethood. It is also said: it means knowledge and understanding. And it is said: it means the Zabur (Psalms). ﴿And decisive speech﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is the decisive judgment between people with truth. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: it is requiring the oath of the defendant and the proof (bayyinah) from the plaintiff. It is also said: it refers to the saying "Amma baʿd" (as for what follows), for he was the first to say it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of fasl al-khitab is the clear speech that the one addressed understands, and this meaning was chosen by Ibn ʿAtiyya, who took it from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾ [al-Tariq: 13].

﴿Has the news of the two litigants reached you, when they scaled the walls of the prayer chamber?﴾ This story is introduced in the form of a question, to alert the listener and to indicate that it is one of the wondrous reports to which one should give close attention. The word khasm (litigant, adversary) applies to one, two, or a group, as in your saying: "'adl" and "zawr." The scholars agreed that these litigants were angels. It is narrated that they were Jibril (Gabriel) and Mika'il (Michael), whom God sent to present a parable to Dawud (David) concerning an incident in which he himself had fallen. He issued a ruling that applied to his own case. When he perceived and understood the intended meaning, he repented and sought forgiveness. We will mention the story after this.

The meaning of "tasawwaru al-mihrab" is that they climbed over its wall and entered it. The mihrab is the highest place in a palace or mosque, and it is the place of worship. It is possible that only two people scaled the mihrab, since the dispute itself was only between two people. In that case, the pronouns in "tasawwaru," "dakhalu," and "faza'a minhum" are used figuratively, and the two are referred to with the plural form. This is permissible according to the view of those who hold that the least number of the plural is two. It is also possible that each of the two litigants had a group with him, so that "khasm" applies to their assembled parties, and the plural pronouns are then used literally. Al-Zamakhshari (may God have mercy on him) relied on this interpretation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 22:

﴿When they entered upon Dawud, and he was startled by them﴾. The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" here is "tasawwaru" (they climbed over the wall). It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh". As for the first "idh", its governing element is "ataka" (has there come to you) or "tasawwaru". Al-Zamakhshari rejected this and said: its governing element is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Has there come to you the news of the litigants when they climbed over the wall?" Dawud was startled by them only because they entered upon him without permission and entered from other than the door. It was also said that this occurred at night. ﴿Two litigants, one of us has wronged the other﴾: the estimated form is "we are two litigants," and the meaning of "baghā" (wronged) is "transgressed". ﴿And do not deviate﴾: that is, do not be unjust toward us in judgment. It is said: "ashatta al-hakim" when the judge acts unjustly. It is recited in the irregular (shadh) reading: "la tushittit" with a fatha on the ta', meaning: do not go far from the truth. It is said: "shatta" when he went far. ﴿To the even path of the way﴾: that is, the middle of the road, meaning the moderate course and the clear truth.

This is the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. He said, "Give it to me to take charge of," and he overpowered me in speech.﴾ This is a narration of the words of one of the two litigants. "Brother" here means brother in religion. The word naʿjah (ewe) in the language applies to the female of wild cattle and to the female of sheep, and here it is an expression for a woman. The meaning of akfilnīhā ("give it to me to take charge of") is: make it mine; its origin is "place it under my guardianship." It has also been said: make it my kafl, that is, my share. The meaning of ʿazzanī fī al-khiṭāb ("he overpowered me in speech") is: he prevailed over me in argument and debate; it is said ʿazza fulān fulānan when he overpowers him. This statement is a parable for the story in which Dawud became involved. People have differed concerning it and have said much about it, both in earlier and later times, to the point that ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever relates what these storytellers (qussas) say about the affair of Dawud (peace be upon him), I will flog him two hadd punishments, because of his violation of the sanctity of one whom Allah has exalted. We will mention from this what is most well known and closest to declaring Dawud (peace be upon him) free of blame. It is narrated that the people of Dawud's time would ask one another to step down from a wife so that he could marry her if she pleased him, and this was a custom among them that they did not reject. Some of this is also reported of the Ansar at the beginning of Islam. It happened that Dawud's gaze fell upon a man's wife and she pleased him, so he asked the man to relinquish her, and he did so. Dawud (peace be upon him) married her, and from her he had Sulayman (peace be upon him). Dawud had ninety-nine wives, so Allah sent to him angels as a parable for his story. One of them said: "Indeed, this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes," indicating that this man had only that one woman. He said: "Give it to me to take charge of," indicating Dawud's request that the man step down from his wife. Dawud (peace be upon him) answered him with the words: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes," and the proof was thereby established against him. At that, the two angels smiled, departed, and were no longer seen. Dawud perceived that this was a reproof from Allah for what he had fallen into.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned in repentance﴾. According to this narration, the story does not imply that Dawud (David), peace be upon him, committed anything that is unlawful in the Shariah. Rather, he was rebuked for something permissible, which he should have avoided because of the elevated rank and the firmness of his religion. The righteous are often rebuked for things for which others are not, as it is said: "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near (to God)." Also, he had ninety-nine wives, and so he was free of this woman. The rebuke therefore fell upon the multiplying of wives, even though it was permissible.

This report is also narrated in another form: David was alone one day in his prayer niche (mihrab) for worship. A bird entered through a window and landed before him, and he admired it. He reached out to take it, but it flew to the window, so David rose to catch it. From the window he saw a woman bathing naked, and she pleased him. Then he left and asked about her, and he was told that she was the wife of a man from his army, who had gone out to fight with the troops. David wrote to the commander of that campaign to send this man forward to fight at the Ark (al-tabut), a place from which few who reached it escaped. The man went forward and fought until he was killed as a martyr. Then David married his wife, and he was rebuked for exposing that man to death, even though he already had ninety-nine other wives. It is said that David intended all of this but did not carry it out, and the rebuke was only for his intention. It is also narrated that the cause of what happened to him was that he admired his own knowledge, and something appeared from him that indicated he did not fear trial for himself, so he was tested through that affair. It is also narrated that the cause was that he wished for the station of his forefathers Ibrahim (Abraham), Ishaq (Isaac) and Ya'qub (Jacob), and he committed himself to being tested as they were tested, so God tested him with what happened to him in that affair.

﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes."﴾ "Su'al" (demanding) is a verbal noun with an object attached to it. It takes "ila" (to) because it implies the meaning of addition, as if he said: "by demanding your ewe be added or joined to his ewes." If it is asked: how did David say to him, "He has certainly wronged you," before that was established for him? The answer is that it is narrated that the other man confessed to this, and his confession was omitted for brevity. It is also possible that his statement "he has wronged you" was made on the assumption that the other's claim was correct. It has also been said that his statement to one of the two litigants, "He has certainly wronged you," before he heard the other's argument, was the sin for which he sought forgiveness and repented.

Surah 38 (Sad), verse 26:

﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor (khalifah) upon the earth﴾. Its implied sense is: God said, "O David." The successorship (khilafah) of David was through prophethood and kingship. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The title khalifat Allah (successor of God) is applied only to a prophet. As for kings and caliphs, each one of them is the successor (khalifah) of the one before him, and the people's saying about them 'the successor of God' is a figurative usage (tajawwuz)."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 27:

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾, i.e., purposelessly. Rather, Allah created them in truth, for people to take heed from them and to draw inference from them concerning their Creator. ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾. The meaning is that when the disbelievers denied the gathering (al-hashr) and the recompense (al-jaza'), the creation of the heavens and the earth was, in their view, vain and devoid of wisdom, since the wisdom in that is only manifested in the recompense of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 28:

﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as those who spread corruption on the earth?﴾ Here "am" (أم) is interrogative, used to express denial: that is, God does not make the believers and the God-fearing like the corrupters and the wicked. Rather, He recompenses each one according to his deeds, so that the wisdom of God in recompense becomes manifest. In this there is an argument for the Gathering (al-hashr) and the Recompense (al-jaza'), and in it there is also a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 31:

﴿When there were displayed before him, in the afternoon, the poised, swift-footed steeds.﴾ Al-ṣāfināt is the plural of ṣāfin, which is the horse that raises one of its legs or forelegs and stands on the tip of the other. It is said that al-ṣāffin is the one that levels its forelegs. Ṣafn (standing poised) is a sign of the horse's excellence, and al-jiyād are those swift in running.

People differed regarding the narrative of this verse. The majority (al-jumhur) said: Sulayman, peace be upon him, was shown horses that he had inherited from his father. It is also said that the devils brought them out for him from the sea, and they had wings, and they numbered a thousand horses. It is also said: he became so occupied with looking at them that the sun set and he missed the afternoon prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿashiyy, i.e. al-ʿaṣr), so he regretted that and said: "Return the horses to me," and he began to strike their necks and hamstrings with the sword until he hamstrung them, because they had been the cause of missing the prayer, and he left only a few of them. God replaced them with something faster than them, which is the wind.

Some scholars denied this report and said: missing the prayer is a sin that Sulayman would not commit, and hamstringing good horses for no benefit is not permissible, so how could Sulayman, peace be upon him, do it? And what sin did the horses commit in causing the prayer to be missed?

Some of them said: he only hamstrung them so that people could eat them, and their time was a time of famine, so he hamstrung them as a means of drawing near to God. Others said: the prayer was not missed, nor were the horses hamstrung. Rather, he was praying, and the horses were displayed before him, so he gestured to them and they were removed until they entered their stables. When he had finished his prayer, he said, "Return them to me," and he began to pass his hand over them, out of honour for them and affection. It was also said that the passing of his hand over them was a marking on their shanks and necks with a mark of dedication in the way of God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 32:

﴿He said, "Indeed, I have loved the good [of horses] over the remembrance of my Lord"﴾ The meaning of this differs according to the differences in the narrative. As for those who said that Solomon slaughtered the horses when he became preoccupied with them until he missed the prayer, they differed on this in three opinions. The first: that "the good" (al-khayr) here refers to the horses, and they claimed that horses are called khayr. "I loved" means "I preferred," or it is taken as a verb that takes min, so the sense is: "I preferred the love of horses, and it occupied me from the remembrance of my Lord." The second: that "the good" here refers to wealth, because horses and other things are wealth; this is like His saying, ﴿If he leaves behind khayr﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], meaning wealth. The third: that the object is omitted, and "love of the good" is a verbal noun, and the estimate is: "I loved these horses with the love of the good, and it occupied me from the remembrance of my Lord." As for those who said that he was praying when the horses were presented to him and he gestured to have them removed, the meaning is that he said: "Indeed, I have loved the love of the good that is with God in the Hereafter, by reason of the remembrance of my Lord, and that occupied me from looking at the horses." ﴿Until they were hidden behind the veil﴾ The pronoun refers to the sun, although it has not been mentioned before; it is understood from the context of the speech, and the mention of "the afternoon" (al-'ashi) requires it. The meaning is: until the sun set. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the horses, and the meaning of ﴿they were hidden behind the veil﴾ is that they entered their stables. The first is more well-known and more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 33:

﴿Bring them back to me﴾ That is, Solomon said: "Bring the horses back to me." ﴿So he began to pass his hand over their legs and necks﴾ Al-suwq is the plural of saq (shin or leg), meaning the legs of the horses; and "their necks" means that he began to pass his hand over them, stroking them. This stroking differs according to the disagreement mentioned earlier: whether it was cutting them and hamstringing them, or passing the hand over them out of affection for them, or branding them to mark them as endowed for the cause of God (tahbis).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 34:

﴿And We did test Solomon, and We placed upon his throne a body; then he turned back in repentance.﴾ The interpretation of this verse differs according to the differing accounts of its story, and on this there are four opinions. The first: Solomon had his ring of kingship, and on it was the name of Allah. He would remove it when he entered the lavatory, out of reverence for the name of Allah, the Exalted. One day he removed it and handed it to a slave-girl, and a jinn took the form of Solomon and asked her for the ring, and she gave it to him. It is related that his name was Sakhr. He sat on Solomon's throne, commanding and forbidding the people, who thought he was Solomon. Solomon went out fleeing for his life, and hunger overtook him, so he asked for a fish, and when it was opened he found his ring inside it, for the jinn had thrown it into the sea. Solomon put on the ring and returned to his kingdom. Thus, according to this view, the trial of Solomon was what befell him of the loss of his kingdom. The body placed upon his throne is the jinn who sat upon it, and he was called "a body" because he took the form of a human being. The meaning of "then he turned back" is that he returned to Allah with forgiveness-seeking and supplication, or that he returned to his kingdom. The second opinion: Solomon had a wife whom he loved, and her father was a disbelieving king whom Solomon had killed. She asked him to make an image of her father, and he complied with this. She would prostrate to the image, and her maidservants would prostrate with her, and it became an idol worshipped in his house, while Solomon did not know until forty days had passed. When he learned of it, he broke it. Thus, according to this view, the trial is the making of the image, and the body is the image. The third opinion: Solomon had a son whom he loved very intensely. The jinn said, "If this son lives, he will inherit his father's kingdom, and we will remain in servitude forever." He was not aware until his son was found dead upon his throne. Thus, according to this view, the trial is his love for the son, and the body is the son when he died, and he was called "a body" because he was a body without a soul. The fourth opinion: he said, "Tonight I will go in to a hundred women, each of whom will bear a horseman who will strive in the way of Allah," and he did not say "if Allah wills." So only one of them conceived, and she bore a half-human. Thus, according to this view, the trial is that he did not say "if Allah wills," and the body is the half-human who was born to him. As for the first opinion, it is weak in terms of transmission, and moreover it is remote from what it mentions concerning the stripping of Solomon's kingdom and the empowering of the devils over him. As for the second opinion, it is also weak, and moreover it is remote that an idol should be worshipped in the house of a prophet, or that a prophet should command the making of an idol. As for the third opinion, it too is weak. As for the fourth opinion, it has been related in a sound hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but the hadith does not state that this is the explanation of the verse.

﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me."﴾ He placed seeking forgiveness before asking for the kingdom, because matters of religion were more important to them than worldly matters, so he gave precedence to what was first and most important. If it is asked, "Why did he say, 'that will not belong to anyone after me'?" The apparent meaning of this is a request for exclusive possession of it, to the extent that al-Hajjaj said of him that he was envious. The answer has two aspects. The first is that he said this so that what happened with the jinn's seizure of his kingdom would not happen to him again. He intended that his kingdom not be taken from him during his lifetime and pass to someone else. The second is that he asked for this so that it would be a miracle, a sign of his prophethood.

﴿So We subjected the wind to him, blowing gently by his command wherever he wished.﴾ The meaning of *rukhā'* (gentle) is mild and pleasant. It was also said that it means obedient to him. We have already mentioned all of this, along with its reconciliation with His words ﴿stormy﴾ in al-Anbiya' [21:81]. *Ḥaythu aṣāba* (wherever he wished) means wherever he intended and willed.

﴿And the devils, every builder and diver,﴾ "the devils" is coordinated with "the wind." "Every builder" indicates the devils: that is, We subjected to him the wind and the devils, those among them who build and those among them who dive in the sea.

﴿And others bound together in shackles,﴾ meaning other jinn who were bound in chains and fetters.

﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold.﴾ The demonstrative refers to the kingdom that Allah gave him. The meaning is that Allah said to him: give to whomever you wish and withhold from whomever you wish. It was also said that the meaning is: release from the shackles whichever of the jinn you wish, and keep in shackles whichever of them you wish. The first is better, and it is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Without reckoning.﴾ This may have three meanings. The first is that he will not be called to account in the Hereafter for what he did. The second is without restriction upon you in your kingdom. The third is without reckoning or counting, rather beyond limit.

﴿And indeed for him with Us is a nearness and a good final return.﴾ This has been mentioned in the story of Dawud.

﴿And remember Our servant Job, when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment."﴾ We have already mentioned the story of Job (peace be upon him) in Surat al-Anbiya' [83]. The word nasb may be read with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād (nuṣb); with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the ṣād (naṣb); with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the ṣād (nuṣub); and with a fatḥah on both (naṣab). Its meaning is one and the same: hardship. If it is asked, "Why did he attribute the affliction that befell him to Satan?" the answer is given in four ways.

The first: the cause of that was from Satan. It is related that he (Satan) entered upon some of the kings, saw an evil act, and did not change it. It was also said that he had a sheep which he slaughtered and cooked, while he had a hungry neighbour, and he did not give his neighbour any of it.

The second: he meant what Satan whispered to him during his illness of impatience and aversion to affliction, so he called upon Allah to repel from him the whispering of Satan by that.

The third: it is related that Allah empowered Satan over him in order to test him. He destroyed his wealth, and he was patient; He destroyed his children, and he was patient; and he was struck by a severe illness, and he was patient. So that was attributed to Satan because Satan had been empowered over him.

The fourth: it is related that Satan met his wife and said to her, "Tell your husband that if he prostrates to me once, I will remove from him the illness he has." The woman mentioned that to Job, and he said to her, "That is the enemy of Allah, Satan." And at that point he called upon (his Lord).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verses 46–48:

﴿Indeed, We made them sincere, with a pure sincerity: the remembrance of the Abode﴾. The meaning of "We made them sincere" (akhlasnahum): We made them devoted to Us, or We singled them out to the exclusion of others. "Khalisa" (pure) is an adjective whose noun has been omitted; its implied form is: "with a quality that is pure." As for the preposition "bi" (with) in His words "with a pure [sincerity]": if akhlasnahum means "sincere" (khalisin), then the "bi" is causal, indicating the reason; and if akhlasnahum means "made them" or "chose them," i.e., "We specified them," then the "bi" is transitive, making the verb take its object.

Nafi' read "khalisati" with an idafa (construct) to "dhikra" (so that it reads "pure [sincerity] of the remembrance of the Abode"), while the rest read it with tanwin (nunation), and others read with tanwin, so that "dhikra" is a substitute (badal) for "khalisa," serving as explanation and clarification of it. As for "al-Dar" (the Abode), it may refer to the Hereafter or to this world. If it refers to the Hereafter, the meaning has three views: First, that "dhikra al-dar" means their remembrance of the Hereafter and Hell within it. Second, that it means their reminding people of the Hereafter and encouraging people toward what is with God. Third, that it means the reward of the Hereafter: that is, We made them pure with the best of what is in the Hereafter. The first is the most evident. If it refers to this world, the meaning is good praise and a fine reputation in this world, like His words: ﴿a tongue of truth﴾ [Maryam: 50; al-Shu'ara': 84].

﴿al-Akhyar﴾: the plural of "khayr" with the yaʾ doubled (khayyar), or "khayr" with the yaʾ lightened, as "mayt" is the lightened form of "mayyit." ﴿And Dhul-Kifl﴾: mentioned in al-Anbiya' [85].

﴿And other punishments of similar kind, in pairs.﴾

"Other" (آخر) is conjoined with "boiling water" (حميم) and "dark, cold liquid" (غساق); the sense is: "and another punishment." It has been said that this refers to al-Zamharir (the bitter, freezing cold). The phrase ﴿مِن شَكْلِهِ﴾ means "of its kind," i.e., of the same type and category as the punishment mentioned. ﴿أَزْوَاجٌ﴾ means "kinds" or "categories," and it is an attribute (صفة) of "boiling water," "dark liquid," and "another punishment." The meaning is that these two are kinds of punishment.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "آخر" is a subject (مبتدأ), and its predicate (خبر) has been disputed. It has been said that the sense is: "and for them is another punishment." It has also been said: "أزواج" is the subject, "من شكله" is the predicate of "أزواج," and the whole clause is the predicate of "آخر." It has also been said: "أزواج" is the predicate of "الآخر," and "من شكله" is in the position of an attribute (صفة). The reading "آخر" in the plural (آخَرُ as أخر، جمع) is also transmitted, and this is more fitting for "أزواج" to be its predicate, because it is the plural of its like.

This is a fawj (a group of people) moving in with you, crowding in and pressing forward. (Note: translating the passage now.)

Let me give the full translation directly.

"This is a host rushing in along with you." Al-fawj (a group of people), and al-muqtahim (one who enters into a crowd and hardship). This is from the speech of the keepers of the Fire (khazanat al-nar), who addressed it to the leaders of the disbelievers who entered the Fire first. Then their followers entered after them, and they are the group referred to. It was said: it is the speech of the people of the Fire to one another, but the first view is more apparent. "No welcome for them!" That is, they will receive no welcome and no good. It is a supplication from the speech of the leaders of the disbelievers: that is, "No welcome for the group who are your followers." "They will say: Rather, it is you who receive no welcome! You have brought this upon us." This relates the speech of the followers to the leaders when they said to them, "No welcome for them," and they replied with their words, "Rather, it is you who receive no welcome." "You brought this upon us." This too is from the speech of the followers addressed to the leaders, and it is the reason (ta'lil) for their words, "Rather, it is you who receive no welcome." The pronoun in qaddamtumuhu refers to the punishment. The meaning of qaddamtumuhu is awjabtumuhu lana, "you made it incumbent upon us," by what you put forward in the world of misguiding us and commanding us to disbelieve.

This is the commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 63:

It is also read with an alif of wasl (hamzat wasl), so that the clause is an attribute (sifah) of "rijal" (men). Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿سِخْرِيّاً﴾ with a damma (sukhriyyan), and the rest read it with a kasra (sikhriyyan). With a damma on the sin, it means "service" from taskhir (subjugation/employment), and with a kasra it means "mockery" (istihza').

﴿أَمْ زَاغَتْ عَنْهُمُ ٱلأَبْصَار﴾ This may carry three aspects. The first is that it is an equivalent (mu'adil) to their saying: "What is it with us that we do not see men?" The meaning is: "What is with us that we do not see them in Hell? Are they not in it, or are they in it but our eyes have swerved away from them?" The meaning of "zaghat 'anhum" (swerved from them) is that they inclined away, so we did not see them. The second is that it is an equivalent to their saying: ﴿أَتَّخَذْنَاهُمْ سِخْرِيّاً﴾, and the meaning is: "Did we take them as objects of mockery?" (Or: "Did the eyes swerve from them?") On this view, it means: the eyes turned away from looking at them, out of contempt for them. The third is that "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), meaning "bal" (rather), with the hamzah (of interrogation), and so it does not equate with anything preceding it.

The pronoun in "He said" here refers to God, Exalted be He. The first *al-ḥaqq* (الحق) is an oath particle (muqsam bihi) in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, as when you say: "Allah, I will certainly do it" (الله لأفعلن). Its response is ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ (لأملأن جهنم), which is in the nominative, either as a subject (mubtada') or as the predicate of a hidden subject, whose estimate is: "The truth is my oath." As for the second *al-ḥaqq*, it is the object of *aqūlu* (أقول, "I say"). His saying ﴿and the truth I say﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumlat i'tirāḍ*, a clause inserted between two parts of a sentence) placed between the oath and its response, for the emphasis of the oath. ﴿And I am not of those who affect (al-mutakallifīn)﴾ means: those who feign and contrive with what is not of their rank.

The pronoun in "He said" here refers to God, Exalted be He. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 38, verse 88:

﴿And you will surely come to know its news after a while﴾. This is a warning: you will surely come to know the truth of his report after a while. The "while" (hin) refers either to the Day of Resurrection, or to their death, or to the manifestation of Islam on the day of Badr and other than it.
